function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 6 — Return Is a Supply Chain
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Query received: 'When can we go home?' Cross-referencing launch manifest database. Estimating response time. Estimating... honesty required."*
     4|
     5|Arun waited until the habitation module was quiet. Not the manufactured quiet of powered-down systems — the real quiet, the kind that settles when twelve people pretend to sleep but are actually listening to each other breathe, each one measuring the weight of the same unspoken question in the recycled air.
     6|
     7|He sat at the engineering workstation, three screens alive with data that nobody else wanted to look at. The numbers had been ready for days. He'd been sitting on them since Earth went quiet, running the calculations a fourth time, a fifth time, a tenth time, because if you're about to tell your team something they don't want to hear, you'd better be right.
     8|
     9|The door cycled. Elena came in first, still wearing her flight jacket, hair pulled back in a knot that had lost its battle with humidity and exhaustion approximately three days ago. Gabriel followed behind her. He'd shaved in front of the mirror that morning. Arun noted this as a small act of defiance — the maintenance of routine when the fundamentals were shifting.
    10|
    11|"You asked us to come down here," Gabriel said, settling into the chair beside Arun's workstation. His voice carried the clipped precision of a military officer who has already decided that whatever he's about to hear, he will handle it. "I'm listening."
    12|
    13|Arun turned the primary screen toward them.
    14|
    15|"I've mapped the supply chain," he said. "Not just our mission. Everything behind it. Every link that has to hold for us to get a return vehicle back to Earth. And I need you to understand what I'm about to show you before we have any conversation about going home."
    16|
    17|Elena pulled a chair close. "Show me."
    18|
    19|The screen filled with a flow diagram. It looked like a subway map designed by someone who had never been underground — lines snaking through orbital assembly stations, fuel depots, manufacturing facilities, training centers, and political decision nodes. Every node carried a number: days to completion, percentage probability, cost in resources that Earth could no longer guarantee.
    20|
    21|"This is a return vehicle launch timeline," Arun said, pointing to the leftmost cluster. "Conception to launch: eighteen to twenty-four months. Minimum. That's if the orbital shipyard at Lagrange Point Two is fully operational and drawing from a supply chain that extends to at least seventeen nations and forty-three private contractors."
    22|
    23|"Twenty-four months," Gabriel repeated. His face didn't change, but Arun saw the calculation happening behind his eyes. They'd been on Mars for fourteen. Add twenty-four. Thirty-eight months total.
    24|
    25|"Minimum," Arun said. "And that's only the vehicle. Now." He tapped a key, and the diagram expanded like a flower opening to reveal its root system. "Here's what feeds the vehicle. Launch vehicle construction requires titanium alloys sourced from three countries. Two are currently embargoed due to the coalition breakdown. The third is running at thirty percent capacity because their workforce has been redirected to atmospheric defense programs in the South China Sea. We don't have titanium."
    26|
    27|"Alternative materials," Gabriel said. It wasn't a question. It was a challenge.
    28|
    29|"We ran the simulations. Aluminum-lithium composites would reduce payload by twenty-two percent. Not enough to carry return fuel and crew life support for the eighteen-month return window. Steel adds too much mass — you can't escape Mars orbit with a steel frame return vehicle. Not with our fuel production capacity."
    30|
    31|Elena leaned forward. "Fuel production. Walk me through that."
    32|
    33|Aru brought up a second diagram. This one showed a chain of chemical processes stretching from raw water ice processing through electrolysis, cryogenic storage, and final propellant loading.
    34|
    35|"Methalox propellant," he said. "Methane and liquid oxygen. We produce it from the CO₂ atmosphere and subsurface water ice. Current production: forty-two kilograms per day. Required to fuel a return vehicle: three hundred twenty metric tons. Simple math says we could produce that in... " He paused, because the number was obscene even to him. "Twenty thousand days. Fifty-four years."
    36|
    37|Gabriel stood. Walked to the wall. Turned around. "There has to be a way to accelerate that."
    38|
    39|"There is," Arun said. "Earth sends us electrolysis arrays. Eight units. Each one increases production by a factor of six. But Earth isn't sending us electrolysis arrays. Earth isn't sending us anything right now because the orbital relay network that coordinates supply drops is down to three functional satellites, and the launch facilities at Cape Canaveral and Kourou are operating on skeleton crews. I have the latest intelligence reports from the last transmission. Kourou hasn't launched in eleven weeks. Cape Canaveral is rationing power."
    40|
    41|Elena's hands were folded on the workstation. She hadn't moved them in a full minute. "What about orbital assembly? Could we build a vehicle from components already in orbit?"
    42|
    43|"That was the original plan," Arun said. "The return vehicle was supposed to be partially assembled at Luna Gateway before mission launch, with final assembly happening during our first year. But the Luna Gateway construction was dependent on a supply chain that stretches through six space agencies and twenty subcontracting firms. When the coalition fractured, the Luna Gateway project was frozen. It's sitting at sixty percent completion. It doesn't have the return stage. It doesn't have the fuel depot. It has a hull and a prayer."
    44|
    45|He let that sit. The numbers on the screen seemed to pulse faintly in the dim light, each one a small truth that together formed an inescapable conclusion.
    46|
    47|"So what you're saying," Gabriel said, his voice level in the way that meant it was taking everything in him to keep it level, "is that there is no return."
    48|
    49|"What I'm saying," Arun corrected gently, "is that there is no return without Earth. The return vehicle isn't just a machine. It's the endpoint of a civilization-scale supply chain. Every bolt, every kilogram of fuel, every kilogram of food reserves for the journey back — all of it depends on Earth functioning as an organized industrial society. And right now, Earth is not functioning that way."
    50|
    51|Elena finally spoke. "How long do we wait?"
    52|
    53|"I don't know," Arun said honestly. "If the coalition stabilizes, if the launch facilities recover, if the orbital supply chain restarts — then maybe we're looking at two years, three years. But I can't model political timelines. I can only model engineering ones. And the engineering says: no Earth, no return. Not the return we planned. Not the return anyone expected."
    54|
    55|*Mission AI: "Addendum: In seventeen months of operation, I have never been asked to model the collapse of an industrial civilization. I have modeled dust storms. I have modeled equipment failures. I have modeled the mathematical probability of finding subsurface ice deposits within fifty kilometers of landing site Epsilon-Seven. I have not modeled this. I am recalibrating my definition of 'impossible.'"*
    56|
    57|---
    58|
    59|Gabriel walked the length of the corridor between the engineering bay and the crew quarters, his boots making the same soft rhythm they'd made every night for fourteen months. Tonight the rhythm felt different. He knew every panel, every cable junction, every scuff mark on the deck plates. This place was a home he had agreed to live in because the agreement included an end date.
    60|
    61|End dates were the foundation of military operations. You deploy for a rotation. You complete the mission. You return. The rotation was eighteen months with possible extension to twenty-four. They were at fourteen. The math he'd been carrying in his head since launch was supposed to resolve in someone else's favor. Now it was just math. Pure, unsentimental, and merciless.
    62|
    63|He found the common area dark except for the ambient glow of the status display on the far wall. Green across the board. All systems nominal. The habitat was functioning perfectly. The irony was not lost on him. They had built a machine that could keep them alive indefinitely in an environment designed to kill them. They just couldn't figure out how to leave.
    64|
    65|Arun was right. He knew Arun was right. The supply chain analysis was thorough, and Arun had never been the type to inflate bad news. If anything, Arun was conservative — the kind of engineer who ran the numbers three times and still hedged his conclusions. If Arun was saying there was no return vehicle coming without Earth's industrial network, there was no return vehicle coming.
    66|
    67|But the question wasn't really about the vehicle. It was about the crew.
    68|
    69|He stood in the common area and watched the status lights pulse. Eleven souls. Well, twelve if you counted the Mission AI, and he did count it — not as a person, but as a presence. Something that had been part of the mission architecture from the beginning and would be part of the ending, whatever form the ending took.
    70|
    71|Some of them would take this differently than others. Chen would want data — she'd be the first to demand Arun's raw calculations. Torres would want action — if there was even a one percent chance, he'd want to be the one pushing for it. Okafor would need time to process. The young geologist had signed up for exploration, not exile.
    72|
    73|The decision in front of him was one he'd been trained for, though not in this context. Tactical communication. Information discipline. When to brief, when to hold, when to frame. The old doctrine said clear and prompt: tell your team the situation, tell them the options, let them respond. But the old doctrine assumed there were options. That there was a path forward that could be executed with courage and discipline and good planning.
    74|
    75|This wasn't that.
    76|
    77|He could tell them now. Lay out the full picture, let them process it as a group, start the conversation about what comes next. That was the honest approach.
    78|
    79|Or he could wait. Wait for one more transmission from Earth. Wait for confirmation that Arun's assessment wasn't just theoretical modeling but reflected an actual policy decision. Wait until he had something to tell them that was more than a mathematical proof of absence.
    80|
    81|He sat in the common area until the status lights cycled through their full rotation — green, green, green, amber for the water reclamation filter that was due for replacement — and back to green. Every system nominal. Every system keeping them alive. Every system tethering them to a planet that had not asked to be their home.
    82|
    83|*Mission AI: "Captain Gabriel Torres — correction, Captain Gabriel is pacing. I have calculated his route. Eighteen passes from engineering to crew quarters. Average velocity: 1.2 meters per second. This is not exercise. This is thinking. I recognize thinking because it is what I do, just with more walking. I would like to note: I think about return approximately 847 times per hour. Not because I want to leave. Because my programming includes a directive to monitor crew wellbeing. And crew wellbeing includes the psychological impact of knowing whether going home is possible."*
    84|
    85|---
    86|
    87|The stabilization sequence for Ship Three took six hours of incremental thrust adjustments, pressure equalization, and structural integrity checks that Arun had personally reviewed three times before giving the thumbs-up. The docking clamps engaged with a sound that vibrated through the habitation module's structural frame — a deep, satisfying thunk that Arun felt in his teeth.
    88|
    89|Ship Three was connected. The full three-ship configuration was operational for the first time since landing. All three vessels were linked by flexible umbilicals, sharing power, data, and thermal regulation. They could sustain the crew indefinitely in triple-ship mode. If one ship suffered catastrophic failure, the other two could support the full crew. They had built redundancy into their architecture from the beginning, because redundancy was the first principle of survival engineering.
    90|

{"content": "# Chapter 7 — The Meeting No One Wanted

*Mission AI: "Crew stress biomarkers elevated across all measurable parameters. Mean cortisol levels up thirty‑eight percent from baseline. Heart rate variability decreased in nine of twelve crew members. Galvanic skin response suggesting anticipatory anxiety. I am tracking these numbers not because anyone asked me to, but because I have been tracking them continuously since Commander Varga closed the door to the engineering bay and did not tell me what she and Arun and Gabriel had decided. This is new. For the first time, I know less than three members of this crew. I do not enjoy this."*

The common area had a capacity of twenty people if you counted standing room. There were twelve crew members today and no one was standing. Chairs were pulled from modules that had never been configured for this many people at once. Someone had dragged Tomas's stool from the robotics bay. Laila had brought her medical tablet and set it face‑down on the table, a gesture she used professionally when she wanted to be fully present rather than distracted by data. It was a small thing but Gabriel noticed it. He noticed everything today.

Elena stood at the front of the room with nothing in her hands. Usually she held a tablet or a pointer — something to occupy her, to signal preparation, to create a barrier between the speaker and the spoken. Today there was nothing. Her palms were bare. Her sleeves were rolled to the elbows. She looked the way people look when there is no armor available and they know it.

Gabriel stood to her left, his own tablet tucked under one arm, the Founding Record — still untitled, still unstarted — waiting in an empty file. He had not slept much. Nobody had, really. The silence from Earth had stretched to fifteen days, and each day of silence had accumulated behind the silence of the ones before it like sediment, layer upon layer, until the floor of the conversation they were all having had risen higher than anyone was willing to acknowledge.

Arun stood against the back wall, arms crossed. He was the one who had built the math. Elena had asked him not to lead this briefing. She had asked him to be present, to answer technical questions, but the delivery of the message was hers. She would not outsource the weight of it to an engineer who had only followed the numbers where they went. She was going to stand in front of the twelve people who had trusted her judgment and tell them that the judgment of every institution that sent them here had been contingent on conditions that no longer obtained.

She waited for them all to settle. Mei was adjusting a chair leg that was slightly uneven. Jonah was leaning against the bulkhead with the deliberate casualness of someone who was preparing to hear something he would not like. Tomas sat with his legs spread and his hands on his knees, his posture open but his jaw tight. Imani sat near the door, always near the door. Laila watched Elena's face the way she watched a patient's face — not just the words, but the micro‑expressions, the tension in the jaw, the breath held a fraction of a second too long before speaking.

"All right," Elena said.

Her voice carried clearly in the small room. She didn't raise it. She didn't need to.

"I've been avoiding this meeting for four days. I avoided it because I wanted better data. I wanted certainty. And the thing about data and certainty when your information is coming from a planet where the infrastructure that produces it is actively breaking down is that you can wait as long as you want and the data isn't going to get better."

She paused. Let the words land.

"I asked Arun to run a full analysis. He did. I asked Gabriel to review the intelligence from our last transmissions. He did. I've reviewed all of it, and I'm going to tell you what we know. Then I'm going to let you respond. I won't manage your response. I won't try to soften the landing. You're adults. You signed up for hard things."

Another pause. Her eyes moved across the faces. All twelve of them. She held each gaze for half a second. Not long enough to be uncomfortable. Long enough to be seen.

"Earth is unstable. I know 'unstable' is a soft word. Soft words are comfortable. I'll use a harder one. Earth's capacity to sustain our return is compromised. The return vehicle that was supposed to be constructed, fueled, and positioned during our first year was dependent on a supply chain that spans orbital assembly infrastructure, fuel depots, manufacturing facilities in at least seventeen nations, and a political coalition that has not functioned as a unified body in eleven weeks."

She let the word eleven hang in the recycled air. Eleven weeks of silence. Eleven weeks of nothing.

"Arun's analysis is clear. The return vehicle depends on Earth. Earth right now is not delivering what it promised. The Luna Gateway orbital assembly is frozen at sixty percent completion. It doesn't have our return stage. It doesn't have our fuel depot. It has a hull. That's it. The raw materials — titanium alloys, specialized electronics, cryogenic storage systems — come from supply chains that are either non‑operational or running at a fraction of capacity. Our own fuel production on Mars, at current rates, would require over fifty years to produce what a return vehicle needs. We do not have fifty years of consumables."

She set her jaw. This was the moment. She could feel it physically, a pressure in her chest that had nothing to do with the air recirculation.

"The odds of our return have sharply fallen. I didn't say they're zero. I said they've fallen. And they have fallen enough that planning for return is no longer the rational way to allocate our time, our energy, or our resources. We have to plan for the alternative. We have to plan for staying."

The silence that followed had mass. Elena could feel it pressing against her. She knew what silence meant after delivering bad news — she'd done it before, in different contexts, with different stakes — but this was different. This wasn't a mission parameter adjustment or a systems failure. This was the ground shifting beneath every expectation every person in this room had brought from Earth.

Nobody moved first. The silence held for six seconds. Seven. Eight.

Then the room fractured.

---

Jonah spoke first. Not with a question, not with an outburst. With a laugh — short, sharp, and entirely humorless.

"Fifty years," he said, looking at the ceiling as if the number might be written there in the acoustic paneling. "Fifty years of making fuel at forty‑two kilograms a day. We can't even fix the number sixteen bearing on the primary water pump because the spare doesn't exist and we don't have a lathe that can cut one to spec. And the plan is — what. We just keep making fuel until the end of our natural lives?"

It wasn't directed at anyone. It was directed at the absurdity of the number itself, the obscene weight of a calculation that turned human time into a fuel production schedule.

Tomas stood then, not in anger but in the restless energy of a man whose instinct is to solve things and who has just been handed a problem that doesn't have a tool. "So the robots," he said. "The robots were the whole point. They were supposed to do the heavy lifting — excavation, construction, regolith moving — so thirty people could do the precision work. But if the robots break down, and we can't get replacements, and we can't manufacture the parts they need —"

"We adapt," Imani said. She was quiet, but her voice cut through the room like a wire through ice. "That's what we do. We adapt or we die. That was always the equation. The only thing that's changed is the timeline."

"The timeline has changed to permanent," Laila said quietly. She hadn't moved from her position. Her face was calm, but her hands were flat on the table, fingers spread, pressing down. She was grounding herself. She'd seen this reaction pattern before — not in space, not on other planets, but in crisis wards on Earth when a diagnosis shifted from manageable to terminal. People didn't panic immediately. They processed. And processing took many forms.

Mei was the one who cried. Not loudly. Not dramatically. A single tear escaped and she wiped it with the back of her hand without acknowledging it, her eyes fixed on the table surface. Her hands were trembling. She'd been quiet through the briefing, absorbing the information through the lens of what it meant for her crops, her seeds, her greenhouse — the one system on this base that required patience, faith, and time that no one had guaranteed and that just became the only thing she had in abundance.

She looked up. "My growing cycles," she said, her voice thick but steady. "The mission plan gave me two full agricultural survey periods. Two. That's twelve growing cycles. I was supposed to optimize yield, send data back, refine my models for the next team. If I'm — if we're staying — I need to plant for calorie density, not for data collection. I need to grow wheat and soy and potatoes, not leafy greens for the psychology experiment. Arun nodded from the back wall. "She's right. The experiment priorities shift immediately."

Patel was staring at his hands. Ramirez was nodding slowly, her lips pressed together. Johansson's eyes were red-rimmed but dry. Mbaye was sitting forward, his physician's face already calculating downstream health impacts. Nakamura was perfectly still. Webb was the one who looked angry.

Webb's voice came out tight, controlled, but threaded with something that Elena recognized as grief being metabolized into rage.

"Nobody is talking about the part that matters. Nobody is talking about the fact that we agreed to this mission because there was an expiration date. We all knew the risks. We signed up knowing Mars could kill us. But we didn't sign up knowing we'd die here."

"Webb," Elena said. She didn't raise her voice. She didn't need to. "I know."

"No, you don't." Webb's hands were clenched. "You're the commander. You get to decide. We get to — what? We get to accept it and start planting potatoes? Where's the conversation about whether we had a choice?"

"You always have a choice," Elena said. "The question is whether the choices are good ones."

"That's not — " Webb stopped. Closed her eyes. Opened them. "I wanted to come home. I told my mother I'd be home. She doesn't know what that means anymore. None of them do."

The room shifted around Webb's statement. It was the raw thing, the unfiltered thing, the admission that everyone was carrying but hadn't yet spoken aloud. Laila watched Webb's posture — shoulders rigid, jaw locked, breathing shallow. Stress response. Acute. Manageable, but if it persisted, she'd need to intervene. Not with medication first. With presence. With the kind of attention a physician gives when the problem is not physiological but existential.

Gabriel had his tablet open now. He was not recording Webb's words directly. He was recording something else — the temperature of the room, the cadence of the reactions, the way the conversation was moving from the personal to the practical, from the raw to the operational. He was thinking about how historians write about moments like this. Not the words that were spoken but the shape of the silence between them. Not the decisions that were made but the weight of the decisions that became impossible.

*Entry,* he typed, though he wouldn't read it back to himself for a long time yet. *Day fourteen. The commander told us. The room held. No one broke. No one left. Everyone began the work of recalculating their life in the space of a single conversation. This is the moment I will mark as the beginning. Not because it was dramatic. Because it was honest.*

He stopped. Deleted the sentence. Rewrote it.

*Entry. Day fourteen. The mission ends today. The colony begins. I am starting this record because someone has to say when the old thing died. If I don't write it down, the date will blur. It always blurs. Years from now, people will ask when the transition happened, and the easy answer — the wrong answer — will be the day of some ceremony or some vote or some formal declaration. It wasn't that. It was this. A room. Twelve chairs. A commander with bare hands. And the truth spoken into air that had been recycled too many times to smell like anything real anymore.*

He set the tablet down.

---

Laila waited until the first wave had passed. She'd read the room the way a physician reads a triage — not by the volume of the complaints, but by the severity beneath them. Webb's anger was acute and would resolve or require intervention. Mei's tears were grief processing and would pass. Tomas's restless energy was problem-solving and would channel itself into work. Jonah's bitter humor was deflection and would persist until he had something concrete to build or fix.

The real question — the question that would determine whether this crew held together or pulled apart in the months ahead — hadn't been asked yet. And she knew, before anyone else spoke, who would ask it. It wasn't Elena. Elena had delivered the message. The next layer belonged to someone else. Someone whose role was not to command but to hold the line between what is and what should be.

Laila stood. She didn't stand for permission. She stood because the weight of the silence was getting heavy and someone needed to apply force in the right direction.

"All right," she said. Her voice was the voice she used in the medical bay when she was about to give someone news that would change the next hour of their life — steady, present, unsentimental but not unkind. "We've got the diagnosis. The prognosis is clear. We're staying. That's the disease. Now. What's the treatment?"

She looked at Elena. The room followed her gaze.

"What changes right now?"

It wasn't a rhetorical question. It wasn't philosophical. It was the one question that separated the crew that would survive from the crew that would dissolve under the weight of knowing something it wasn't prepared to act on.

Laila didn't move from her position. She waited. Her face was still the face of a physician — clinical, attentive, but behind the clinical she carried her own weight. The knowledge that her medical supplies had a shelf life. That her capacity to treat trauma, chronic disease, dental emergencies, psychological crises, and the slow accumulation of radiation damage over years — not months, years — was bounded by what they'd packed in sealed crates and brought across a hundred million kilometers. She was carrying the knowledge that every pill she dispensed was one pill closer to zero, and no one was coming to replenish her shelves.

Elena looked at Laila with an expression of profound gratitude. She hadn't known she needed the question to be asked, but she had needed it. The question that pivots from what is to what must be done. The question that turns a verdict into a plan.

"Everything," Elena said.

She stepped forward. Closer to the table, closer to the crew. The barrier was gone now. No tablet, no podium, no distance.

"Let me go through it. System by system. Because the way we've been running this base — the way Mission Planning told us to run it, the way we trained to run it — it's designed for a two-year mission with a clean exit ramp. Every decision was optimized for that. If we're staying, we have to un-optimize everything and re-optimize for permanence. And I want everyone to understand what that means."

She turned to the wall display. It was already showing the mission overview — green across the board. All systems nominal. The irony of the green lights was almost funny, if the situation weren't so serious.

"First. EVA hours. Our standard EVA allocation is eight hours per crew member per week. That's based on the assumption that we complete our primary surface work within twenty-four months and that suit wear is manageable within that window. But Imani has already flagged that suit degradation is outpacing mission models. Dust is getting into joints, seals are wearing faster than expected, and the bearings Imani replaced last week are showing micro‑abrasions after three uses, not thirty. If we're staying indefinitely, we can't burn through our suit inventory at this rate. I'm proposing we cut standard EVA hours to six per week per person, with mandatory rotation through suit maintenance assignments. Imani will brief the new EVA doctrine separately."

Imani nodded. She'd already drafted half of it. The other half would come from what they'd learned during the next dust season, and the season after that.

"Second. Food assumptions. Mei, you've already started thinking about this. I need you to shift your entire growing cycle to calorie density. Leafy greens for morale — yes, keep some. But the priority is wheat, soy, potatoes, legumes. We need caloric yield, not data yield. Our current food stores cover us for approximately thirty months with careful rationing. Thirty months sounds like a lot until you realize we've been here fourteen. We have sixteen months to go from hydroponic supplementation to full agricultural self-sufficiency. If we don't hit that window, the math gets very unforgiving."

Mei was already writing. Her hands had stopped trembling. The tears were gone, replaced by the fierce, quiet focus of a biologist who has just been given the parameters for the most important growing cycle of her life. "I need to expand the greenhouse footprint by at least twenty percent. That means repurposing the secondary storage bay. It means reallocating power for grow lights. It means water —"

"We'll get to water," Elena said. "Stay with me."

"Third. Maintenance cycles. We are currently running preventive maintenance on all major systems at the intervals specified in the mission manual. Those intervals assume a two-year lifespan for equipment. If we're staying longer, we have to extend our maintenance cycles in ways that weren't designed into the original specs. That means more frequent inspections, more aggressive replacement of marginal components, and most importantly —" she turned to Jonah "— we need a formal fabrication program. If something breaks and we don't have a spare, we can't wait for it. We build it. Jonah, I need you on lead for this. You'll coordinate with Arun on what we can manufacture in-house and what we absolutely cannot replicate."

Jonah's expression shifted. The bitterness from before was still there, but it was being forged into something harder and more useful. Anger was a fuel, and Jonah Mercer was a man who knew how to burn it. "What do I have to work with?" he asked.

"The machine shop. The fabrication tools we brought for contingency repair. And the scrap yard we're about to create from experimental equipment that no longer serves its original purpose. You'll tell me what you can build, and I'll allocate the resources to get you the raw material."

"Fourth." "Power margins. We are currently operating at roughly eighty-two percent of our total generation capacity under normal conditions. That gives us an eighteen percent margin for demand spikes, system failures, and dust events. Eighteen percent is not enough for permanent habitation in an environment where every single piece of critical infrastructure degrades over time and none of it can be replaced from off-site. We need to expand our power generation. Arun —"

Arun uncrossed his arms. "I've been running the scenarios. We can increase solar efficiency by twenty percent if we reconfigure the panel tilt algorithm for our actual latitude and dust accumulation rates instead of the theoretical optimal from the mission plan. We can also commission the Sterling generator as a more active part of our power mix — not just as backup, but as a load-balancing system that runs during peak demand. But both of these require engineering hours we're currently spending on science experiments."

"Exactly," Elena said. "Which brings me to the fifth point. Experiment priorities."

The word hung in the room for a moment. Experiment. It was a word from the old life, the life of visiting scientists with a return ticket and a deliverable to show for their time.

"We came here to do science. Geology, atmospheric research, biology, materials science, radiation mapping — the mission included a full research program designed to fill gaps in our understanding of Mars. That was the justification for our payload allocation. That's how we explained ourselves to the public and to the agencies that funded us."

She looked around the room.

"That science matters. But it doesn't matter right now. We're not sending data back to researchers who are actively waiting for it. We don't know if the receiving institutions still exist. So I am suspending all non-critical experiments effective immediately. The radiation mapping that we've been doing for three months? Suspended. The atmospheric composition study? Suspended. The regolith mineral analysis? Suspended."

Nakamura flinched. She was the atmospheric scientist. Three months of work, sitting on her tablet in an archived folder that nobody on Earth would ever access, because the people who had assigned her that work were probably not at their desks anymore.

"What stays," Elena continued, and here her voice shifted — not softer, but more precise, like a laser cutting through noise, "is the science that directly supports permanent habitation. Mei's agricultural optimization stays. Arun's life-support efficiency studies stay. Laila's long-term health monitoring stays. Gabriel's communication and archival work stays. Everything else is on hold. Not cancelled permanently. On hold. If and when Earth stabilizes, if and when we re-establish regular communication, we'll reassess. But until then, every watt of power, every hour of labor, every liter of water goes to the things that keep us alive and the things that build the infrastructure to stay alive."

She paused. Her hands were on the edge of the table now, leaning forward, her face close to the center of the room.

"I know this is a lot. I know none of this is what you trained for. But I want to be very clear about what I'm asking. I'm not asking you to give up. I'm asking you to change the shape of what you're doing. The skills you brought to this mission — the engineering, the botany, the medicine, the mechanics, the piloting, the fabrication, the historical documentation — all of those skills are more important now than they were when the mission plan included a return date. Because now the skills aren't just about collecting data and going home. They're about building a life."

She straightened up. Her voice softened, just a fraction.

"I know you brought things. Photographs. Books. Drawings your children made. Clothes your spouses packed. Recipes for meals you wanted to eat when you got home. I know what those things mean. I have a photograph of my father, and I've looked at it four times since I came into this room, trying to figure out how to tell him that his daughter is not coming back. I haven't figured it out. Maybe I'll find a way. Maybe I won't."

She let that sit. Not to manipulate. To be honest. To show them that she was carrying the same grief, the same weight, the same impossible recalculation that each of them was making in the privacy of their own minds.

"But I will figure it out," she said. "And in the meantime, I will run this colony the way I know how. With competence. With honesty. And with the full understanding that every decision I make from this point forward is not about a mission with an end date. It's about a place with a future. Our future."

She looked at Laila. Laila nodded, once. The nod said: *You gave them the diagnosis. Now they can process the treatment.*

The questions came after. Not panicked questions. Not angry questions, even though the anger was still in the room, banked like coals under ash. Technical questions. Practical questions. We have approximately eighteen months of surgical supplies, twenty-four months of basic pharmaceuticals, and — here's the constraint — six months of specialized medications. She was feeling the conversation shift now — the energy of the room moving from reaction to action, from the vertigo of new information to the solid ground of work that needed to be done. This was what she had needed. This was what she had hoped would happen. Not cheerfulness. Not acceptance. Webb was quiet now. She had stopped clenching her fists. Her breathing had settled. Laila tracked her with a physician's eye and judged: acute crisis passed. Grief would return in waves. Seventy-two hours. An arbitrary number, she knew. But it served a purpose: it gave everyone a deadline, a structure, a reason to get up tomorrow morning and do something instead of sitting in their bunk thinking about the photograph in their locker and the mother they'd told they were coming home.

When the meeting ended, nobody rushed for the door. They filed out slowly, some still asking each other questions, some silent. Mei was already talking to Laila about the possibility of growing medicinal plants alongside food crops. Tomas was walking beside Imani, comparing notes on robot reallocation. Jonah stood by the door for a long moment, watching them all, his expression a complex map of reluctance, determination, and the particular gravity of a man who realizes he is about to become the most important person in the room when anything breaks.

Gabriel stayed. He and Elena stood together in the common area after the last crew member had left — Tomas, who had paused at the door to say, in a voice that was rougher than usual, "We'll figure it out, Commander. We always do."

"Not always," Elena had said, and he'd laughed, a short genuine sound that told her more about his state than any biomarker reading could.

Gabriel tapped his tablet. The screen showed the first entry of the Founding Record, the one he'd written during the meeting, the one he was still editing.

*What do you think?* he asked her, not about the writing but about the moment.

"I think," Elena said slowly, "that we just did the thing you can only do once. You can only announce the end of the old mission once. Everything from here on is something else."

Gabriel nodded. "A colony. Not because I said it. Because the moment we stopped planning a return and started planning a future, the word became true."

He looked down at his tablet. Beneath the first entry, he began to type a second one. Not for anyone. For the record.

*Day fourteen. The commander told the crew. The crew did not break. The crew asked what changes. She answered. In the space between the question and the answer, the old mission ended quietly, without ceremony or violence, and the new thing began. It did not look like a colony. It looked like twelve people in a room making plans. But it was a colony. It was born here. In this room. At this hour. I am writing it down because the first thing a civilization needs is a record of its own beginning. Even if the beginning looks like an engineer's supply chain analysis and a physician's pragmatic question and a commander with nothing in her hands but the truth.*

He looked up. "Someone has to say when the old mission died," he said quietly. "If I don't write it, the date gets lost. The date matters."

Elena looked at him. For the first time since she'd entered the room, she smiled. Not a broad smile. Not a happy one. But a human one, the kind that exists not in spite of difficulty but because of the particular weight of sharing it with someone who understands.

"Then write it," she said. "Write it all."
